title: Rye and Caraway Bread
subtitle: a dense, flavourful loaf with Northern European character
excerpt: Dark rye flour gives this loaf a close, chewy crumb and a pleasantly sour edge. Caraway seeds run through every slice. It is the bread to serve with smoked fish, strong cheese, or a good bowl of soup.
sourceNotes: Inspired by German and Scandinavian rye breads, adapted for the home oven.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice before freezing. Rye bread keeps well in the freezer.

content.text: Rye dough is stickier than wheat dough and will not develop the same elasticity when kneaded. Do not try to make it smooth -- a rough, tacky dough is correct. Shape it with wet hands and do not overwork it.

items.prepNote: use 250g dark rye flour and 150g plain flour

content.text: Mix the yeast with the warm water and honey. Leave 5 minutes. Combine the rye flour, plain flour, salt, and caraway seeds in a large bowl.
Add the yeast liquid. Mix to form a sticky, cohesive dough. It will not be smooth -- this is normal for high-rye doughs.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 hour. The dough will not double dramatically, but it should visibly expand and feel lighter.
With wet hands, shape into a log and place in a greased 900g loaf tin. Smooth the top with wet fingers. Cover and leave for 30 minutes.

Heat the oven to 200C. Slash the top of the loaf with a sharp knife. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the loaf sounds hollow when tapped. Cool fully before slicing -- rye bread slices better once completely cold.

items.symptom: Loaf is very dense and barely rose
items.cause: High rye content reduces rise. Some density is expected, but too little rise suggests under-fermentation.
items.fix: Give the first prove longer if the dough feels cold. Rye ferments more slowly than wheat.

items.symptom: Loaf is gummy when sliced warm
items.fix: Do not cut until the loaf is completely cold. Leave it for several hours or overnight.

content.text: Rye bread is staple throughout Northern and Eastern Europe. Germany alone has hundreds of regional rye loaves. The caraway seed combination is particularly common in Scandinavian and German baking. In Britain rye bread occupies a quieter place -- more delicatessen than everyday bakery -- but its flavour complexity rewards the effort.
